query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Post-synthesis isothermal annealing near the recrystallization temperature will induce controlled nanoprecipitation at the internal boundaries of the dual-phase lamellar colonies in eutectic high‐entropy alloys, forming a ductile interphase that both impedes microcrack initiation and contributes precipitation strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase (e.g., FCC/B2) lamellar colonies characterized by numerous brittle internal boundaries prone to microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a carefully tuned isothermal annealing treatment immediately after solidification to promote nanoprecipitate formation specifically along the internal lamellar boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions are maintained, and the annealing parameters are optimized to retain the dual-phase lamellar architecture (avoiding excessive grain growth or phase coarsening).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoprecipitates (or a ductile interphase) selectively formed at the internal boundaries
generation.mechanism: The formation of a ductile nanoprecipitate phase at the boundaries will enhance interfacial cohesion, reducing microcrack nucleation and propagation, while the precipitates also provide precipitation strengthening. This dual action is predicted to simultaneously increase yield strength and improve tensile ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified, as-cast lamellar alloy, the annealed alloy will exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased elongation to failure under room-temperature testing.
generation.baseline: The unmodified eutectic high‐entropy alloy showing brittle behavior due to microcrack initiation at numerous internal boundaries under tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if annealing is performed at temperatures near the recrystallization point for an optimized time; deviation from these parameters (i.e., excessive annealing leading to grain coarsening or inadequate annealing failing to produce nanoprecipitates) could negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise annealing temperature and time window necessary to reliably form the desired nanoprecipitates without degrading the lamellar architecture are not yet defined and require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high‑entropy alloy samples from the same batch. Subject one set to the proposed isothermal annealing treatment near the recrystallization temperature while keeping the other set as a control (processed via conventional methods). Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM) to verify nanoprecipitate formation along the lamellar boundaries and conduct room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: Nanoprecipitate presence, size, and distribution at internal boundaries (via TEM/SEM)
Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength (via room-temperature tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a significant and localized formation of nanoprecipitates at the internal boundaries and/or fail to manifest simultaneous improvements in both strength and ductility relative to the control samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. chosen.technique: isothermal annealing to induce nanometer-scale ductile interphase formation at lamellar boundaries
chosen.conditions: annealing at a temperature near recrystallization for a short duration in an inert atmosphere to ensure uniform interfacial precipitation without bulk coarsening
chosen.why: This move directly targets the performance limitation by focusing on engineering the internal boundaries—the known microcrack initiation sites—through a standard thermal treatment. Prior studies in similar dual-phase and high-entropy systems have shown that enhancing interface toughness can simultaneously improve strength and ductility. This intervention, by forming a ductile interphase at the lamellar boundaries, is expected to blunt crack propagation and elevate strain hardening, thus offering a straightforward, testable way to falsify the hypothesis via mechanical testing against an unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys established that the inherent dual-phase lamellar (fcc/B2 or L12+B2) structures can yield high strength and ductility under certain conditions. Subsequent studies then applied various thermomechanical processes (e.g., severe cold/warm rolling, hybrid deformation, dual annealing cycles) to refine and heterogenize the microstructure, which not only inherited the lamellar architecture but also introduced nanoprecipitates and dual heterogeneous zones. These efforts improved overall strength–ductility synergy, yet none have fully overcome the issue of microcrack initiation at the multitude of brittle internal boundaries.
decision.unsolved: Despite successfully increasing strength via grain refinement and precipitation, the problem of boundary-initiated microcracking under room-temperature tensile deformation remains. The challenge is to reinforce the internal boundaries with a beneficial, ductile interphase without altering the key dual-phase lamellar morphology that confers the alloy’s high strength.
decision.why: Building on the trend of using thermal treatments to precisely modify the microstructural features, the next logical step is to apply a well-controlled post-solidification thermal treatment near the recrystallization temperature. This intervention is designed to trigger controlled nanoprecipitation specifically at the dual-phase lamellar boundaries, thereby forming a ductile interphase that can arrest the propagation of microcracks while maintaining the beneficial lamellar architecture. This approach directly targets the unresolved brittleness resulting from internal boundaries, occupies a niche aligned with previous efforts to improve interface properties, and offers a testable hypothesis wherein the absence of the targeted nanoprecipitates upon deviation from the tuned thermal conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
